title: Make Other People Come to You - Use Bait If Necessary

chapterBreakdown.gentle: This law says that chasing other people often means accepting their timing and field. Greene treats movement itself as a strategic concession. If the other person has to come toward you, they usually reveal interest, spend effort, and adjust first. That is why bait matters. A small opportunity, invitation, or visible opening can pull someone into motion without blunt force. The chapter is not praising passivity. It is about arranging a better field so the other side crosses toward it. Movement then starts favoring your structure instead of theirs, and the approach itself becomes useful information about what matters to them. But the tactic has limits. Bait that is obvious, desperate, or too costly can expose anxiety instead of control. The real goal is to make approach happen on terms you shaped rather than to get trapped designing schemes that still leave you reacting.
chapterBreakdown.direct: This law argues that power grows when other people move toward your position instead of making you chase them on theirs. Movement is not neutral here. The person who advances first often gives up tempo and reveals need. Greene therefore treats bait as a way to control approach. An offer, opening, or inducement can make the other side cross distance on ground you prefer. That is stronger than pursuit because it preserves initiative and makes their effort part of your structure. But the chapter is not about doing nothing. Passive waiting is not control. The tactic only works if the invitation actually shapes the field and gives the approach strategic value from the start. It also breaks when the bait is too obvious or too expensive and turns the operator back into the reactive party again. The key is chosen ground, not frozen silence.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Greene's eighth law says that chasing is often a hidden surrender. The moment you run after someone else's timing, you are already playing on their field. Power grows when they have to cross toward you instead. That is why bait matters. A useful opening, tempting offer, or visible gap can pull the other side into motion while you keep initiative. The point is not laziness. It is architecture. You want contact to happen on ground you arranged, with their movement already paying part of the cost and revealing real interest before you do. But bad bait blows the move up fast and ruins the angle. If the lure looks needy, costs too much, or still leaves you reacting, then you did not control movement at all. You just built a fancier version of pursuit. Winning here means making the crossing serve your board.

point.competitive: Whoever runs first usually gives something up.

oneMinuteRecap.gentle: This law treats movement as part of power. When others approach your chosen ground, you usually keep more initiative than when you chase them on theirs.

oneMinuteRecap.competitive: Do not sprint onto someone else's board if you can make them step onto yours.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Greene begins this law by treating pursuit as a hidden weakness. The person who keeps chasing often accepts the other side's timing, urgency, and terrain before the exchange is even defined. That is why movement matters. It is not only physical distance. It is a sign of who is adapting first, and often of who feels more need to close the gap.

This makes movement itself strategic. If the other side has to approach you, they usually spend the first unit of effort, reveal what they want, and begin adjusting to your field. Greene's point is not that standing still is automatically wise. Passive waiting can be weakness too. The stronger move is to shape conditions so their approach serves your structure and makes your field the easier one to enter.

Bait is the mechanism for doing that. It can be an opening, an inducement, an apparent opportunity, or a visible gap that gives the other side a reason to move. The chapter treats bait less as blunt trickery than as controlled invitation. Someone approaches because the field has been arranged to make approach feel attractive or necessary, not because you openly dragged them there.

That distinction matters because it keeps the law from collapsing into passivity. The operator is not doing nothing. The operator is designing the board. A good lure changes tempo and position without shouting the tactic out loud. It makes movement look like the other side's choice while still preserving your initiative.

The chapter becomes practical in ordinary settings very quickly. A manager can structure access so requests arrive on chosen terms. A fair booth can be arranged so others cross toward it instead of needing to be chased. A tense personal exchange can be handled by making the return path calmer and more attractive than continued distance. In each case, the board is doing strategic work before words fully begin.

But the limit matters. Bait that is obvious, too expensive, or emotionally transparent can fail and reveal anxiety rather than control. Once the lure becomes clumsy, the operator may still end up reacting to the response. The law is strongest when it preserves initiative, not when it turns into complicated self-trapping. If the bait still leaves you adapting, the architecture was weaker than the chase.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
This chapter argues that chasing others usually means surrendering initiative before the real contest begins. The person who moves first often accepts the other side's timing and ground. Greene treats that as a strategic concession because it gives the other party more control over how contact unfolds and more evidence about how badly you want the exchange.

That is why movement matters so much here. If you can make the other side come toward you, they spend effort first, reveal interest first, and start adapting to your structure first. The chapter is not praising stillness for its own sake. It is praising control over approach and the tempo that follows from it.

Bait is how that control gets built. Greene uses it broadly: an opportunity, invitation, inducement, or opening that makes the other party want to move. Once they move, the board is no longer neutral. The approach itself has already shifted tempo in your favor, because they are now crossing into conditions you prepared.

This is why bait is stronger than blunt pursuit when it works. A direct chase lets the other side keep setting terms. A controlled lure makes them cross into a field you prepared. The difference is not passivity versus action. It is action through architecture. The lure changes the board before the exchange is fully visible.

The law shows up in plain modern settings. Access systems, meeting structures, offer timing, and even emotional tone can all function as bait when they make the other side reopen contact on your timetable. The common feature is induced movement rather than donated movement. The point is to make their approach do some of the strategic work for you.

But Greene keeps a hard limit near the surface. Obvious bait, overcostly bait, or bait that reveals too much need can reverse the advantage. The operator then looks manipulative, anxious, or trapped by their own design. The tactic only works while approach stays under your terms rather than turning you reactive again. If the lure becomes a confession of dependence, it is just pursuit in a smarter costume.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Greene's eighth law starts with a cold read on pursuit: when you chase, you usually give up the board before the game is properly underway. The other side keeps its timing, its field, and its emotional frame while you spend energy crossing toward it. That is why movement is not neutral. It often signals who is already adapting and who is already paying from need.

The chapter flips the problem by treating approach as something to force onto others. If they have to move toward you, they spend the first effort, show their hand sooner, and start working inside your structure. That is leverage. It is not stillness. It is control over who has to cross the distance and who gets to receive the crossing.

Bait is the tool that creates that movement. Greene uses it as inducement: an apparent opportunity, opening, or invitation that makes the other side choose motion. Once they choose it, they are no longer fully on their own ground. The board has already shifted, and their movement is already helping your position.

For that reason, controlled invitation can beat open pursuit. Chasing lets the other person keep setting the frame. Lure them in instead, and the frame starts bending toward you. The chapter is really about architecture, not inactivity. You build the path they will want to step onto.

You can see the mechanism anywhere initiative matters. Structure the request path so others come to your process. Design the offer so they reopen on your terms. Create a more attractive return route in a strained relationship. In every case, the gain comes from making their movement do some of your work. Their crossing becomes part of your leverage.

But the tactic goes bad fast when the bait is obvious, expensive, or nervous. Then the lure stops looking like control and starts looking like need. At that point you are back in reaction, only with extra embarrassment attached. The law works only while the board still feels like yours. If the trap starts shouting hunger, the chase was merely disguised.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
This chapter begins by redefining pursuit as a concession rather than as pure effort. When you keep chasing another person, opportunity, or conflict, you usually accept more than motion. You accept their timing, their emotional frame, and often their preferred ground. Greene treats that acceptance as a strategic loss because initiative is already being spent before the visible contest has properly started.

That is why movement matters so much in this law. The person who advances first often reveals need first, adapts first, and gives the other side more information about what matters to them. By contrast, the person who can hold position while inducing approach usually keeps more control over tempo and structure. The chapter is therefore not about distance by itself. It is about who is paying the movement tax.

Bait is Greene's mechanism for shifting that tax. He uses it broadly enough to include inducement, apparent opportunity, invitation, or a visible opening that makes the other party choose motion. The aim is not crude deception for its own sake. The goal is to build conditions under which approach feels natural, beneficial, or urgent to the other side while still serving your arrangement.

This is what makes the law more sophisticated than passivity. The operator is not simply waiting and hoping. The operator is shaping the board. Good bait creates a field that attracts movement while preserving the ability to receive that movement on prepared terms. It converts architecture into leverage.

That leverage appears in ordinary settings with surprising clarity. Access can be structured so others must reopen contact through your process. Opportunities can be timed so the other side has to step toward your calendar instead of dragging you into theirs. Emotional distance can be arranged so return feels easier than continued avoidance. In each case, the gain comes from making their movement do some of your strategic work.

But bait has a failure line. If it becomes too obvious, too costly, or too emotionally transparent, it stops looking like control and starts looking like dependence. The other side may resist, exploit the reveal, or simply watch you become trapped in the mechanism you designed. This is the chapter's main limit. Not every inducement preserves initiative. Some inducements merely disguise pursuit more elaborately.

For that reason, Greene's law cannot be reduced to "never move first." Some situations require direct action, some opponents will not bite, and some windows close if you keep waiting for perfect conditions. The stronger reading is narrower: when movement can be induced rather than donated, the person who sets the field usually keeps more initiative. When it cannot, forward motion may still be the better trade.

Chapter 7 showed how visible ownership gets attached to results once the audience is already watching. Chapter 8 moves even earlier and asks who controls the terms of contact before the result exists at all. The real question is exact: when does making others come toward your chosen ground create leverage, and when does the bait itself reveal too much anxiety, cost, or need? The serious answer is to use inducement only when it preserves initiative more cleanly than pursuit would, and to abandon the tactic the moment it stops making movement serve your field.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Greene's eighth law says that chasing is often a hidden surrender. The person who keeps running after the other side usually accepts the other side's timing, field, and emotional frame before the exchange has properly begun. That is why pursuit can weaken position even when it feels energetic.

The chapter treats movement as a strategic resource. Whoever crosses first often reveals more need, spends more effort, and adapts sooner. Whoever can induce approach instead usually keeps more initiative. This is not a mystical claim about stillness. It is a claim about who is forced to adjust to whose structure.

Bait is the tool that shifts that adjustment. Greene uses the term broadly: inducement, opportunity, invitation, or opening that makes the other side move toward your ground. The aim is not fake passivity. The aim is to structure conditions so their approach helps your position instead of your pursuit helping theirs.

In that sense, the law is really about architecture. The operator builds a field in which approach feels worthwhile or necessary to the other side. Once the other side takes the step, the board is already less neutral. Tempo and structure have started moving in your favor, and their movement is already telling you something about need and priority.

The mechanism appears in practical settings all the time. You can design access so others must reopen through your process. You can time an offer so they return on your calendar. You can create conditions in a strained relationship that make re-entry easier than continued distance. In all these cases, approach is being induced rather than donated. The field is doing strategic work before the exchange fully hardens.

But the tactic has a visible failure mode. Obvious bait, overcostly bait, or bait that reveals too much need reverses the advantage. Then the inducement starts advertising dependence, manipulation, or anxiety. The operator may still be reacting, only now from inside a more embarrassing design. A failed lure can reveal more weakness than a clean direct move would have shown. Bad architecture can be worse than an honest chase. It can also teach the other side exactly how exposed your position really is. It may even hand them a map of your leverage problem.

This is why the law cannot be reduced to passive waiting. Some situations demand forward action. Some targets will not move. Some opportunities expire. Greene's harder claim is conditional: when you can make others come to your field without revealing too much need or paying too much for the lure, you usually keep more control than you would by chasing. When that condition disappears, the cleaner move may still be forward. Chosen ground has to stay genuinely chosen.

Chapter 7 dealt with who gets remembered once the result is visible. Chapter 8 asks who controls the ground before the result exists at all. The hard question is when induced approach is preserving initiative and when it is merely pursuit wearing a smarter costume. The move works only while the lure keeps the field yours.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
This law starts with a blunt correction: chasing is often surrender in motion. The minute you keep running at someone else's timing, you are already paying to play on their board. Greene treats that as weakness because movement often reveals need before the contest is even visible.

That is why the chapter cares so much about who crosses first. The first mover often spends effort first, adapts first, and shows where the hunger is. The stronger position is to make the other side cross toward you instead. Then their movement starts working for your structure instead of your movement working for theirs.

Bait is the mechanism that creates that reversal. Greene uses it as inducement: an opening, opportunity, or tempting structure that makes the other side choose motion. Good bait does not simply fool. It makes approach feel worthwhile while keeping the board tilted toward you.

This is why the law is about architecture, not idleness. The operator builds a field that attracts movement. Once the other side steps in, tempo and position have already shifted. Their choice to approach has done part of the strategic labor for you, and it has already made them adjust before you do.

You can see the pattern anywhere initiative matters. Set the process so requests come through your route. Time the offer so they return on your calendar. Make the return path in a strained relationship easier than continued absence. In each case, their movement starts paying the tax you would otherwise have paid. The board is doing work before the argument starts.

But the lure can betray the operator fast. If the bait is obvious, expensive, or needy, the board flips back. Now the inducement advertises anxiety instead of control, and the other side either resists it or uses the reveal against you. That is pursuit in disguise, and disguise does not save it. A loud lure can confess your hunger in one move. The reveal may hand them more leverage than the bait ever promised you. Sometimes it even trains them to wait for your overreach. At that point the board is working for them.

So Greene is not saying never move. Some doors do not reopen on their own. Some opponents refuse the lure. Some windows close while you are busy admiring your own setup. The harder claim is narrower and smarter: when you can make them cross toward your field at lower cost than chasing them on theirs, do it. When you cannot, move directly without pretending a failed lure was strategy. The board has to keep paying you back.

Chapter 7 was about who gets the crown once the result is visible. Chapter 8 moves earlier and asks who gets to build the board before the result exists at all. The hard question is whether your bait is truly making their movement serve you or merely hiding your own chase inside a prettier structure. The law pays only while the board still belongs to you.

twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Today, stop one unnecessary chase and build one better return path instead.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Before the day ends, redesign one board so they have to cross instead of you.

weeklyPractice.gentle: For one week, track where you donated movement, where others crossed toward you, and what each pattern did to initiative.
weeklyPractice.direct: Spend seven days auditing who moved first, who set the field, and when bait preserved or lost control.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Run a one-week movement audit and see who keeps paying the tax in your world.

front.gentle: Why can chasing others weaken position in this chapter?

back.gentle: Because chasing often means accepting the other side's timing and field.
back.direct: Pursuit usually donates initiative before the exchange is settled.
back.competitive: You start paying the movement tax the moment you run onto their board.

front.gentle: What does bait do in this chapter?
front.direct: How does inducement help control movement?
front.competitive: What is the lure really buying?

back.gentle: It gives the other side a reason to approach on terms you shaped.
back.direct: Bait shifts movement by making the other party cross toward your field instead of you chasing them.
back.competitive: It makes their motion start doing your work.

front.gentle: Why is the law not just about waiting passively?
front.direct: What separates induced approach from doing nothing?

back.gentle: Because the operator still has to shape a field that rewards approach.
back.direct: Control comes from architecture, not from idle stillness.
back.competitive: If you did not build the board, you are not really making anyone step onto it.

front.direct: When does inducement collapse into reaction?
front.competitive: What gives the board away again?

back.gentle: Bait fails when it becomes too obvious, too costly, or too emotionally transparent.
back.direct: The tactic breaks when the lure exposes need and still leaves you reacting to the response.
back.competitive: A needy lure turns control back into chase.

front.gentle: What hard limit keeps this law from becoming a rule against all direct action?
front.direct: Why can't the law mean never move first?

back.gentle: Because some situations require direct initiative and some lures simply will not work.
back.direct: The law is conditional: induced approach is stronger only when it preserves initiative more cleanly than pursuit would.
back.competitive: If the board will not pull them in, the clean move may still be forward.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Do not donate movement carelessly. The stronger move is often to shape a field that makes others approach on your terms.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Initiative often belongs to the side that controls approach, not to the side that chases hardest.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: If you can make them cross your board instead of sprinting onto theirs, take that trade.
